podcast.body: Joy Division had a pact: if anyone left for any reason, the band would break up. When singer Ian Curtis hanged himself from his kitchen doorframe on May 18, 1980 — the night before a North American tour that could have broken the band internationally — the three surviving members honored the dissolution but immediately reconstituted under the name New Order. Curtis was 23. After everyone took turns at vocals, guitarist Bernard Sumner was designated singer in late July 1980; Stephen Morris's girlfriend Gillian Gilbert was added on keyboards that fall, completing the classic lineup. "Blue Monday" — their biggest single — was built by accident from a drum machine left running while the band tried to leave the stage early; a missed programmed note became a happy accident. The most successful 12-inch in history, it lost money on every copy sold due to the expensive die-cut packaging. The name Blue Monday refers to the Monday after Ian Curtis died by suicide the previous Sunday. "New order made it cool to dance again."

podcast.body: New Order were devising a way to leave the stage early without audiences noticing, by running Stephen Morris's drum machine through the end of their set. They added sequenced keyboard parts and a bass line, and before long had the foundation of a complete song — all written by machines. The full recording session took place while the band was loaded on LSD; the engineers sent them to a café across the street to finish mixing in peace. During production, Gillian Gilbert accidentally missed programming one note in the melody, leaving it slightly out of time with the rhythm track — a mistake they kept because it sounded better. "Blue Monday" was released only as an 8-minute 12-inch single and became the best-selling 12-inch in music history. However, the elaborate die-cut packaging was so expensive to produce that New Order and the label lost money on every copy they sold. "New Order had the foundations of a new song, and it was all being played entirely by machines."

podcast.body: New Order's "Blue Monday" was released as an eight-minute, 12-inch single, gaining its biggest traction in dance clubs. It became the top-selling 12-inch single globally, selling over three million copies. Despite its massive success, Factory Records lost 30 pence for every copy sold due to excessive investment in the sleeve's intricate design and printing, leading to losses of "tens of thousands of pounds." "New orders blew Monday, the top selling 12-inch single in the history of the universe, three million plus copies, yet it lost money."

podcast.body: This iconic 8-minute 12-inch single originated from New Order's reluctance to perform encores. They devised a plan to turn on Stephen Morris's drum machine and walk off stage to drink backstage. The concept evolved with a sequencer triggering Gillian Welch's keyboards and Barney Sunder suggesting sequencing Peter Hook's bass lines, thus forming the entirely machine-played foundation of a new song. Legend has it the band, reportedly under the influence of LSD, recorded the tracks, after which the studio engineer, seeking peace, sent them to a cafe on Croc's Street to finish mixing. Upon its release, it gained radio play but had its most profound impact in dance clubs, dramatically shifting the landscape of dance music, making dancing "cool again," and forging crucial links between new music, rock, and dance. "Blue Monday" sold over 3 million copies, establishing it as the best-selling 12-inch record in the history of Planet Earth. Ironically, the elaborate artwork and cover for the single were so expensive to produce that New Order lost one pence on each copy sold, resulting in a total loss of 30,000 pounds for issuing "the world's favorite dance record." "Blue Monday sold over 3 million copies and it's still the best selling 12-inch record in the history of Planet Earth."

podcast.body: A mistake by Gillian Gilbert during the programming of this song's intro led to it becoming New Order's greatest hit and the biggest 12-inch remix ever. Steven Morris had programmed the drum machine intro, and Gillian's role was to trigger a sequencer playing a melody. She accidentally omitted a note, causing her part to be out of sync with the beat. Instead of correcting it, the band, reportedly under the influence of LSD, decided to keep the mistake as it created an "interesting tension" in the song. "And a mistake by Jillian helped turn one particular New Order song into their greatest hit. Steven had programmed a drum machine to be the song's intro. Jillian's part came next and her job was to trigger a sequencer playing a melody. But because she forgot to put one note into her programming, her part was out of sync with the beat. But rather than change it, New Order apparently was looped on acid at the time. They just left it as it was because the mistake created some interesting tension within the song."
